nodes.name: contact toric manifold
nodes.statement: A {\em contact toric manifold} of dimension $2n-1$ is a compact connected $(2n-1)$-dimensional contact manifold equipped with an effective Hamiltonian action of an $n$-torus $T^n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
differentia: equipped with an effective Hamiltonian action of an $n$-torus $T^n$

nodes.name: Lerman's classification theorem of contact toric manifolds
nodes.statement: Lerman gave a full-classification theorem of contact toric manifolds in \cite{L:contact toric}. According to Lerman's theorem, when $n\geq 3$ and the torus action is not free, the contact toric manifolds are classified by their {\it moment cones}, which by definition are the union of $\{origin\}$ and the moment map image of their symplectizations. These moment cones are all {\it good cones}.
nodes.statement_short: Non-free contact toric manifolds with $n\geq 3$ are classified by their moment cones, which are good cones.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
assumptions: when $n\geq 3$ and the torus action is not free
conclusions: the contact toric manifolds are classified by their {\it moment cones}
These moment cones are all {\it good cones}.

nodes.name: good cone
nodes.statement: A {\bf good cone} in $\R^n$ is a rational polyhedral cone given by \begin{equation} C= \bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in \R^n: \langle x, v_{i}\rangle \geq 0\}, \end{equation} where $F_{i}=\{x\in \R^n: \langle x,v_{i} \rangle=0\}$ is a facet of $C$ and $v_{i}\in \Z^n$ is the inward-pointing primitive normal vector to $F_{i}$. In addition this cone must satisfy: (i)For $0<l<n$, each codimension $l$ face $F$ of $C$ is contained in exactly $l$ facets: \begin{equation*} F=F_{i_{1}}\cap F_{i_{2}}\cap\cdots\cap F_{i_{l}}; \end{equation*} and (ii) The $\Z$-module generated by $v_{i_{1}},...,v_{i_{l}}$ is a direct summand of $\Z^n$ of rank $l$.
nodes.statement_short: A rational polyhedral cone whose codimension-$l$ faces lie in exactly $l$ facets, with the corresponding normals spanning a rank-$l$ direct summand of $\Z^n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
differentia: (i)For $0<l<n$, each codimension $l$ face $F$ of $C$ is contained in exactly $l$ facets
(ii) The $\Z$-module generated by $v_{i_{1}},...,v_{i_{l}}$ is a direct summand of $\Z^n$ of rank $l$.

nodes.name: good contact toric manifold
nodes.statement: A contact toric manifold $M$ is called a {\bf good contact toric manifold} if $dim M > 3$ and the moment cone of $M$ is a strictly convex good cone.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
differentia: the moment cone of $M$ is a strictly convex good cone

nodes.name: Strict convexity is equivalent to Reeb type
nodes.statement: The requirement that the moment cone being strictly convex is equivalent to asking $M$ to be of {\em Reeb type}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Contact toric manifolds with non-strictly-convex moment cone
nodes.statement: When the moment cone is not strictly convex, the construction of contact toric manifold with the given moment cone can be found in the proof of Proposition 4.7 in \cite{LS:integrable torus actions}. They are topologically $T^k\times S^{k+2l-1}$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.origin_citation: Lerman & Shirokova, Completely integrable torus actions on symplectic cones

nodes.name: Borel construction
nodes.statement: Assume $G$ is a Lie group and $M$ is a topological space with a $G$-action. Let $EG$ be a contractible topological space with a free $G$-action. Then $G$ acts freely on $EG\times M$ diagonally. The quotient space of this action, which we will denote by $(EG\times M)/G$ and $EG\times_{G}M$ interchangeably, is called the {\em Borel construction} of the $G$-space $M$.
nodes.statement_short: The quotient $(EG\times M)/G$ of $M$ by a free diagonal $G$-action on $EG\times M$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: equivariant cohomology
nodes.statement: The {\em equivariant cohomology} of $M$ is defined as the ordinary cohomology of $EG\times_{G}M$ and is denoted $H_{G}^{*}(M)$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Equivariant cohomology of a point
nodes.statement: The equivariant cohomology of a point is thus a polynomial ring with $m$ variables, i.e, \begin{equation} H_{T^m}^{*}(pt;\Z) = \Z[x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{m}], \end{equation} where $x_{i}\in H^{2}_{T^m}(pt;\Z)$.
nodes.statement_short: $H^{*}_{T^m}(pt;\Z)$ is the polynomial ring on $m$ degree-two generators $x_i$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: the polytope $P$ cut out by the hyperplane $H$
nodes.statement: The intersection of $C$ with the hyperplane \begin{equation} H = \{(x_{1},...,x_{n})\in \R^n : x_{n}=1\} \end{equation} is a simple rational convex polytope. We denote it by $P$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Smoothness Criterion
nodes.statement: {\bf Smoothness Criterion:} The polytope $P$ is a Delzant polytope in $H$, and the vector $(v_{i1},v_{i2},...,v_{i,n-1})$ is primitive in $\Z^{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $P$ is Delzant in $H$ and each truncated normal $(v_{i1},\dots,v_{i,n-1})$ is primitive.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Delzant polytope
nodes.statement: a Delzant polytope is by definition a smooth simple rational convex polytope
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: symplectic toric manifold
nodes.statement: A $2n$ dimensional {\bf symplectic toric manifold} is a compact connected symplectic manifold equipped with an effective Hamiltonian action of an $n$-torus $T^n$.

nodes.name: Delzant's classification of symplectic toric manifolds
nodes.statement: Delzant showed in \cite{Delzant} that these geometric objects are classified by their moment image, which is a simple rational smooth polytope, called a {\bf Delzant polytope} in the symplectic literature.
nodes.statement_short: Symplectic toric manifolds are classified by their moment image, a Delzant polytope.

nodes.name: toric symplectic cone
nodes.statement: A {\bf toric symplectic cone} is the symplectization of a contact toric manifold. Toric symplectic cones and contact toric manifolds are in one-to-one correspondence.
nodes.section: 2 Basic definitions, constructions and examples
nodes.origin_citation: Lerman, Geodesic flows and contact toric manifolds
nodes.genus: symplectization of a contact toric manifold

nodes.name: characteristic map
nodes.statement: A {\bf characteristic map} is a map \begin{equation*} \lambda: \F\rightarrow \Z^l \end{equation*} where $\Z^l$ is the integral lattice in $\R^l$. Here $l$ and $n$ are not necessarily equal. Denote $\lambda(F_{i})$ by $\lambda_{i}$.
nodes.section: 2 Basic definitions, constructions and examples

nodes.name: the equivalence relation $\Delta$ determined by $\lambda$ and the space $P^{\lambda}$
nodes.statement: Every finite subset $U$ of $\Z^l$ determines a subgroup of $T^l$ generated by \begin{equation*}\{(e^{u_{1}\theta},e^{u_{2}\theta},...,e^{u_{l}\theta}):\theta\in \R,(u_{1},...,u_{l})\in U\}\end{equation*} It is in fact a closed subgroup. For every point $p$ in $P$(or $C_{0}$), denote by $S^{\lambda}_{p}$ the subgroup of $T^l$ determined by vectors \begin{equation*}\{\lambda_{i}:p\in F_{i}\}.\end{equation*} Define an equivalence relation $\Delta$ on $T^{l}\times P$ by: \begin{equation} (g,p)\Delta (h,q) \Leftrightarrow p=q, and\ g^{-1}h\in S^{\lambda}_{p}. \end{equation} We say $\Delta$ is the equivalence relation determined by $\lambda$. Let $\Delta_{p}$ denote $S^{\lambda}_{p}$, and $P^{\lambda}$ denote the quotient space $(T^{l}\times P)/\Delta$. With the quotient topology and the $T^{l}$ action on the first coordinate by multiplication, $P^{\lambda}$ is in the category of $T^{l}$-topological spaces.
nodes.statement_short: Glue $T^l\times P$ by collapsing, over each point $p$, the subtorus $S^{\lambda}_{p}$ generated by the $\lambda_i$ of the facets containing $p$.
nodes.section: 2 Basic definitions, constructions and examples

nodes.name: Combinatorial model $C_{0}^{\lambda}$ of a toric symplectic cone
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} C= \bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in \R^n: \langle x, v_{i}\rangle \geq 0\} \end{equation} be a strictly convex good cone in $\R^n$. The vector $v_{i}$ is the inward-pointing primitive normal vector to $F_{i}$. We assume the equations are {\bf minimal}; that is, removing any one of the equations will give a different set. We will always assume that the equations used to define convex polytopes or cones are minimal. We let $C_{0}=C\backslash \{origin\}$. We set $l=n$ and define a characteristic map $\lambda$ by $\lambda(F_{i})=v_{i}$. We denote by $\Delta$ the equivalence relation on $T^n\times C_{0}$ determined by $\lambda$. Then $C_{0}^{\lambda}= (T^n\times C_{0})/\Delta$, with $T^n$ acting on the first coordinate by multiplication, is $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to a toric symplectic cone. This claim will be proved in Section~\ref{sec:equi contact}.
nodes.statement_short: Taking $\lambda(F_i)=v_i$ on a strictly convex good cone gives $C_{0}^{\lambda}$, a model of the toric symplectic cone.
nodes.section: 2 Basic definitions, constructions and examples

nodes.name: Combinatorial model $P^{\lambda}$ of a good contact toric manifold
nodes.statement: For $C$ as in the previous example, it is a cone over a simple convex polytope $P$. Notice that the facets of $P$ are in one-to-one correspondence with those of $C_{0}$. We let $\tilde{F_{i}}$ denote the facet of $P$ contained in $F_{i}$. We may define a characteristic map as in Example~\ref{ex:symplectic cone combina} by sending $\tilde{F_{i}}$ to $v_{i}$. By abuse of notation,we still call this map $\lambda$ and denote by $\Delta$ the equivalence relation on $(T^n\times P)$ determined by $\lambda$. We emphasize that $\lambda_{i}= \lambda(\tilde{F_{i}})$ is the normal vector to $F_{i}$, not to $\tilde{F_{i}}$ in $P$. Then $P^{\lambda}= (T^n\times P)/\Delta$, with $T^n$ acting on the first coordinate by multiplication, is $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to the contact toric manifold $M$ associated to $C$. The space $C_{0}^{\lambda}$ in the previous example is the symplectization of $M=P^{\lambda}$. These claims will be proved in Section~\ref{sec:equi contact}.
nodes.statement_short: The same normals $v_i$ applied to the facets of the base polytope $P$ give $P^{\lambda}\cong M$.
nodes.section: 2 Basic definitions, constructions and examples

nodes.name: Combinatorial model $P^{\tilde{\lambda}}$ of a symplectic toric manifold
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a Delzant polytope, i.e. a convex simple rational smooth polytope, in $\R^{k}$ given by \begin{equation} P = \bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in \R^k: \langle x, \tilde{v_{i}}\rangle \geq \eta_{i}\}.\end{equation} The equations are again assumed to be minimal, as in Example~\ref{ex:symplectic cone combina}. We denote the $i^{th}$ facet by $\tilde{F_{i}}$. Then $\tilde{v_{i}}$ is the inward-pointing primitive normal vector to the facet $\tilde{F_{i}}$. We set $l=k$ and define a characteristic map $\tilde{\lambda}$ by setting $\tilde{\lambda}(\tilde{F_{i}})= \tilde{v_{i}}$. Denote by $\tilde{\Delta}$ the equivalence relation on $T^k\times P$ determined by $\tilde{\lambda}$. Then $P^{\tilde{\lambda}}=(T^k\times P)/\tilde{\Delta}$, with $T^k$ acting on the first coordinate by multiplication, is $T^{k}$-equivariantly homeomorphic to the symplectic toric manifold associated to $P$. This will be restated in Section~\ref{sec:symplectic orbifold}.
nodes.statement_short: For a Delzant polytope with normals $\tilde{v_i}$, $P^{\tilde{\lambda}}$ models the associated symplectic toric manifold.
nodes.section: 2 Basic definitions, constructions and examples

nodes.name: Relation to Davis-Januszkiewicz quasitoric manifolds
nodes.statement: In their paper \cite{DJ}, Davis and Januszkiewicz defined a class of manifolds equipped with torus action which they called {\em toric manifolds}, now called {\em quasitoric manifolds}, and computed their equivariant and ordinary cohomology rings. The cohomology ring of symplectic toric manifolds is a particular example of the cohomology ring of a quasitoric manifold. Quasitoric manifolds are a strictly larger class than symplectic toric manifolds. More information may be found in \cite{GP:quasitoric}. Constructions in \cite{DJ} were later generalized to orbifolds in \cite{PS:quasitoric orbifolds}.

nodes.name: the maps $\pi_{\Z},\pi_{\R},\pi_{T}$ and the subgroup $K=\ker(\pi_{T})$ of a good cone
nodes.statement: Define a map \begin{equation} \pi_{\Z}: \Z^m\rightarrow \Z^n \end{equation} by sending the $i^{th}$ standard basis vector $e_{i}$ of $\Z^m$ to $v_{i}$. This induces a map \begin{equation} \pi_{\R}: \R^m\rightarrow \R^n \end{equation} by tensoring with $\R$. We then get a map \begin{equation} \pi_{T}: T^m=\R^m/\Z^m \rightarrow T^k=\R^n/\Z^n \end{equation} The subscripts $\Z,\R,T$ may be omitted when it will not cause confusion. Let $K=ker (\pi_{T})$. Then we have a short exact sequence of groups \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ 1 \ar[r]^{} & K \ar[r]^{i} & T^m \ar[r]^{\pi_{T}} & T^n \ar[r]^{} & 1 . }
nodes.statement_short: Send $e_i\mapsto v_i$ to get $\pi_\Z,\pi_\R,\pi_T$, and let $K=\ker\pi_T$, giving $1\to K\to T^m\to T^n\to 1$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds

nodes.name: Moment map $\nu$ of the $T^n$-action on the symplectic cone $S$
nodes.statement: This action is Hamiltonian with moment map \begin{eqnarray} \nu: & S& \rightarrow (\mathfrak{t}^n)^{*}\\ &[z_{1},...,z_{m}]& \mapsto (\pi^{*})^{-1}(u(z_{1},...,z_{m})), \end{eqnarray} using that $\pi^{*}$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: $\nu[z]=(\pi^{*})^{-1}(u(z))$ is the moment map of $T^n$ on $S$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds

nodes.name: Lerman's description of the toric symplectic cone associated to $C$
nodes.statement: Lerman showed in \cite{L:contact toric} that \begin{equation} S=((i^{*}\circ u)^{-1}(0)\backslash \{0\})/K \end{equation} is the toric symplectic cone associated to $C$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
assumptions: C= \bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in \R^n: \langle x, v_{i}\rangle \geq 0\}
conclusions: S=((i^{*}\circ u)^{-1}(0)\backslash \{0\})/K

nodes.name: $C_{0}^{\lambda}$ is $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to the symplectic cone $S$
nodes.statement: With the same notation as in Example~\ref{ex:symplectic cone combina}, $C_{0}^{\lambda}$ is $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to $S$, the symplectic toric cone associated with $C$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
assumptions: With the same notation as in Example~\ref{ex:symplectic cone combina}
conclusions: $C_{0}^{\lambda}$ is $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to $S$, the symplectic toric cone associated with $C$

nodes.name: Proof that $C_{0}^{\lambda}\cong S$
nodes.statement: If we restrict the domain of $u$ defined in \eqref{eq:std moment contact} to \begin{equation}(\R^m)^{+}=\{(z_{1},...,z_{m})\in \C^m: z_{i}\in \R_{\geq 0},\forall i\},\end{equation} it is a homeomorphism onto its image. Call this restriction map $u_{0}$. Now define a map \begin{equation}\gamma_{0}: T^n\times C_{0}\rightarrow S\end{equation} by: \[(t_{n},p)\mapsto t_{n}.[u_{0}^{-1}(\pi^{*}(p))]\] We note that $\pi^{*}(p)\in (\R^m)^{+}$ because of the defining equations for $C$. Thus, $u_{0}^{-1}(\pi^{*}(p))$ is well-defined, and it is straightforward to check that \begin{equation*}u_{0}^{-1}(\pi^{*}(p))\in (i^{*}\circ u)^{-1}(0)\backslash \{0\}.\end{equation*} We let $[u_{0}^{-1}(\pi^{*}(p))]\in S$ be the equivalence class of $u_{0}^{-1}(\pi^{*}(p))$. Finally, $t_{n}\in T^n$ acts on $S$ as noted earlier. This map $\gamma_{0}$ is a continuous. It is also surjective because $C_{0}$ is the orbit space of the $T^n$-action on $S$. According to Lemma~\ref{lemma:stabilizer}, which will be stated and proved right after this proposition, $\gamma_{0}$ induces a bijective map \begin{equation} \gamma: (T^n\times C_{0})/\Delta\rightarrow S\end{equation} The inverse of this map is also continuous since $\gamma$ is an open map. Finally, $\gamma$ is obviously $T^n$-equivariant.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\gamma_0$ from the inverse of the restricted moment map, then descend it to a $T^n$-equivariant homeomorphism using the stabilizer lemma.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds

nodes.name: Stabilizer lemma
nodes.statement: The stabilizer of $[u_{0}^{-1}(\pi^{*}(p))]\in S$ is $\Delta_{p}\leq T^n$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
conclusions: The stabilizer of $[u_{0}^{-1}(\pi^{*}(p))]\in S$ is $\Delta_{p}\leq T^n$

nodes.name: Proof of the stabilizer lemma
nodes.statement: For simplicity and without loss of generality, we may assume that the facets that contain $p$ are exactly $F_{1},...,F_{j}$. Thus, the coordinates of $\pi^{*}(p)$ that are zero are exactly the first $j$ coordinates. Consequently, the stabilizer of $[u_{0}^{-1}(\pi^{*}(p))]$ must be $$ \{ \pi_{T}(e^{i\theta_{1}},e^{i\theta_{2}},...,e^{i\theta_{j}},1,1,...,1): \theta_{1},...,\theta_{j}\in \R\}.$$ This is precisely $\Delta_{p}$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume WLOG that the facets through $p$ are $F_1,\dots,F_j$ and read off the vanishing coordinates.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds

nodes.name: $P^{\lambda}$ is $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to $M$
nodes.statement: Let $M$ denote the good contact toric manifold associated to $C$. With the same notation as in Example~\ref{ex:contact combina}, $P^{\lambda}$ is $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to $M$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
assumptions: Let $M$ denote the good contact toric manifold associated to $C$.
With the same notation as in Example~\ref{ex:contact combina}
conclusions: $P^{\lambda}$ is $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to $M$

nodes.name: Proof that $P^{\lambda}\cong M$
nodes.statement:
By definition, the symplectic cone $S$ is the symplectization of $M$. Topologically, $S= M	imes \R$. The map $
u$ defined in \eqref{eq:moment toric } is proportional on the second coordinate. For each $q\in M$, there is a unique $x=x(q)\in \R$, such that $$
u(q,x(q))\in P .$$ Notice that $P^{\lambda}=(T^n	imes P)/\Delta$ is a subset of $(T^n	imes C_{0})/\Delta$, so $(T^n	imes P)/\Delta$ is $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to its image under $\gamma$ as defined in \eqref{eq:gamma}. This is precisely the pre-image of $P$ under $
u$, which is $$\{(q,x(q))\in S=M	imes \R : q\in M\}.$$ This is clearly $T^n$-equivariantly homeomorphic to $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Cut the symplectization $S=M\times\R$ by the level set $\nu^{-1}(P)$, which is a graph over $M$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds

nodes.name: the characteristic map $\mu$ and the Davis-Januszkiewicz space $P^{\mu}$
nodes.statement: Define a characteristic map \begin{equation} \mu :\tilde{\F}\rightarrow \Z^m \end{equation} by sending $\tilde{F_{i}}$ to $e_{i}$, the $i^{th}$ standard basis vector of $\Z^m$. Denote by $\Omega$ the equivalence relation on $T^m\times P$ determined by $\mu$. This space $P^{\mu}=(T^m\times P)/\Omega$ was first defined in \cite{DJ}.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
nodes.genus: the equivalence relation on $T^m\times P$ determined by $\mu$

nodes.name: $P^{\mu}$ is a $K$-bundle over $P^{\lambda}$
nodes.statement: $P^{\mu}$ is a fiber bundle over $P^{\lambda}$ with fiber $K$, where $K$ was defined in \eqref{eq:KT^mT^n}.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
assumptions: $K$ was defined in \eqref{eq:KT^mT^n}
conclusions: $P^{\mu}$ is a fiber bundle over $P^{\lambda}$ with fiber $K$

nodes.name: Proof that $P^{\mu}\to P^{\lambda}$ is a $K$-bundle
nodes.statement: The group $K$ acts naturally on $P^{\mu}=(T^m\times P)/\Omega$ by multiplication on the first coordinate. Since $C$ is a good cone, $K\cap \Omega_{p}=1$ for every $p\in P$. Thus the $K$ action on $P^{\mu}$ is free. The orbit space is exactly $P^{\lambda}=(T^n\times P)/\Delta$. The projection from the total space to the orbit space is given by the natural map \begin{eqnarray*}\pi':& P^{\mu}=(T^m\times P)/\Omega&\rightarrow P^{\lambda}=(T^n\times P)/\Delta\\ &[t_{m},p]&\mapsto [\pi_{T}(t_{m}),p].
nodes.statement_short: Goodness of $C$ gives $K\cap\Omega_p=1$, so the $K$-action is free with orbit space $P^{\lambda}$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds

nodes.name: Splitting of $T^m\to K_{0}$
nodes.statement: There exists a group homomorphism $r: T^m\rightarrow K_{0}$, satisfying $r\circ i|_{K_{0}}=id_{K_{0}}$, where $id_{K_{0}}$ denotes the identity map on $K_{0}$ and $i$ is the inclusion of $K$ into $T^m$ as defined in \eqref{eq:KT^mT^n}.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
assumptions: $i$ is the inclusion of $K$ into $T^m$ as defined in \eqref{eq:KT^mT^n}
conclusions: There exists a group homomorphism $r: T^m\rightarrow K_{0}$, satisfying $r\circ i|_{K_{0}}=id_{K_{0}}$

nodes.name: Proof of the splitting $r:T^m\to K_{0}$
nodes.statement: Consider the maps\[\xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r]^{} & ker(\pi_{\Z}) \ar[r]^{j} & \Z^m \ar[r]^{\pi_{\Z}} & \Z^n },\] where $\pi_{\Z}$ is defined in \eqref{eq:pi_Z contact} and $j$ is the inclusion map. As a subgroup of the free abelian group $\Z^m$, $ker(\pi_{\Z})$ is also a free abelian group. So with suitably chosen basis, the map $j$ looks like an inclusion \[b_{1}\Z\oplus b_{2}\Z\oplus \cdot\cdot\cdot \oplus b_{k}\Z \hookrightarrow \Z\oplus\Z\oplus \cdot\cdot\cdot \Z\oplus \Z^{m-k}.\] But notice that for every $x\in \Z^m$ and every $t\in \Z\backslash\{0\}$, \[x\in ker(\pi_{\Z})\Leftrightarrow tx\in ker(\pi_{\Z}).\] So all of the $b_{i}$ must be $1$. This means $ker(\pi_{\Z})$ is a direct summand of $\Z^m$, so there is a group homomorphism \begin{equation} r_{0}:\Z^m\rightarrow ker(\pi_{\Z}),\end{equation} such that \[r_{0}\circ j = id_{ker(\pi_{\Z})}.\] This $r_{0}$ induces a map \begin{equation} r: T^m\rightarrow K_{0} \end{equation} that satisfies the requirement of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: $\ker\pi_\Z$ is saturated in $\Z^m$, hence a direct summand, and the retraction $r_0$ exponentiates to $r$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds

nodes.name: $EK_{0}$-bundle comparison lemma
nodes.statement: The space $(EK_{0}\times ET^n)\times_{T^m}((T^m\times P)/\Omega)$ is a fiber bundle over\\ $ET^n\times_{T^n}((T^n\times P)/\Delta)$ with fiber $EK_{0}$. Thus these two spaces are homotopy equivalent.
nodes.statement_short: The $T^m$-Borel construction of $P^{\mu}$ built from $EK_{0}\times ET^n$ fibers over the $T^n$-Borel construction of $P^{\lambda}$ with contractible fiber.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
conclusions: The space $(EK_{0}\times ET^n)\times_{T^m}((T^m\times P)/\Omega)$ is a fiber bundle over\\ $ET^n\times_{T^n}((T^n\times P)/\Delta)$ with fiber $EK_{0}$
Thus these two spaces are homotopy equivalent.

nodes.name: Proof of the $EK_{0}$-bundle comparison lemma
nodes.statement: Define the projection map by \[[x,y,[t,p]]\mapsto [y,[\pi(t),p]],\] where $x\in EK_{0}$, $y\in ET^n$, $t\in T^m$, $p\in P$. The square brackets $[\ ]$ are used whenever there is a equivalence relation involved. It is easily shown that the map is well-defined. As for the fiber, pick any point $[y_{0},[t_{n},p]]$ in the base space, with $y_{0}\in ET^n$, $t_{n}\in T^n$, $p\in P$. Assume $[x,y,[t,p]]$ is in the pre-image, then \[[y,[\pi(t),p]]=[y_{0},[t_{n},p]].\] So there exists $s\in T^n$ such that \[sy=y_{0},\ \ \ \mbox{and}\] \[[s\cdot\pi(t),p]=[t_{n},p].\] Since $\pi_{T}$ is surjective, so there is an $s'\in T^m$ such that $\pi(s')=s$. Then \[[x,y,[t,p]]=[r(s')x,\pi(s')y,[s't,p]]=[r(s')x, y_{0}, [s't,p]],\ \mbox{and}\] \[ \pi'[(s't),p]=[\pi(s')\pi(t),p]= [s\cdot\pi(t),p]= [t_{n},p],\] where $\pi'$ is defined in Lemma~\ref{lemma:fiberK}. This means when considering the fiber over $[y_{0},[t_{n},p]]$, we only need to use representatives of the form $[x,y_{0},[t,p]],$ where $y_{0}$ is fixed, and $\pi'[t,p]= [t_{n},p]$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:fiberK}, we know that the set of points $[t,p]\in P^{\lambda}$ that satisfy $\pi'[t,p]=[t_{n},p]$ is homeomorphic to $K$. The elements in $T^m$ that fix $y_{0}$ are $K$. So the fiber over $[y,[t_{n},p]]$ is homeomorphic to $(EK_{0}\times K)/K$, which is homeomorphic to $EK_{0}$ via the map \[[x,k]\mapsto r(k)^{-1}x,\] noticing that $K$ acts on $EK_{0}$ by first mapping $k\in K$ to $r(k)\in K_{0}$, then applying $r(k)$ to $EK_{0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the fiber over a base point with $(EK_{0}\times K)/K\cong EK_{0}$ using the retraction $r$.

nodes.name: Homotopy equivalence of the two Borel constructions
nodes.statement: The two spaces \begin{equation} (EK_{0}\times ET^n)\times_{T^m}((T^m\times P)/\Omega) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} ET^m\times_{T^m}((T^m\times P)/\Omega) \end{equation} are homotopy equivalent.
nodes.statement_short: Replacing $ET^m$ by $EK_{0}\times ET^n$ does not change the homotopy type of the Borel construction of $P^{\mu}$.

conclusions: The two spaces \begin{equation} (EK_{0}\times ET^n)\times_{T^m}((T^m\times P)/\Omega) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} ET^m\times_{T^m}((T^m\times P)/\Omega) \end{equation} are homotopy equivalent.

nodes.statement: Define $\I$ to be the ideal of $\Z[x_{i},x_{2},...,x_{m}]$ or $\Q[x_{i},x_{2},...,x_{m}]$ generated by monomials \begin{equation*}\left\{x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{l}}: \bigcap_{j=1}^{l}\widetilde{F_{i_{j}}}=\emptyset\right\}.\end{equation*} The coefficients used will be clear in context.

nodes.name: Equivariant cohomology of a good contact toric manifold
nodes.statement: If $M$ is the contact toric manifold associated with the strictly convex good cone \[C= \bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in (t^{n})^{*}=\R^n: \langle x, v_{i}\rangle \geq 0\}\] then \[H_{T^n}^{*}(M;\Z)\simeq \Z[x_{1},...,x_{m}]/\I,\] where $x_{i}\in H^{2}_{T^n}(M;\Z)$.
nodes.statement_short: The $T^n$-equivariant cohomology of $M$ is the Stanley-Reisner ring $\Z[x_1,\dots,x_m]/\I$ of its moment cone.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
assumptions: If $M$ is the contact toric manifold associated with the strictly convex good cone \[C= \bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in (t^{n})^{*}=\R^n: \langle x, v_{i}\rangle \geq 0\}\]

nodes.name: Proof of the equivariant cohomology theorem
nodes.statement: According to Lemma~\ref{lemma:EK0 bundle},\[H_{T^n}^{*}(M;\Z)=H^{*}(ET^n\times_{T^n} P^{\lambda},\Z)= H^{*}((EK_{0}\times ET^n)\times_{T^m}P^{\mu};\Z)\] According to Lemma~\ref{lemma:AG Property}, they are equal to \[H_{T^m}^{*}(P^{\mu};\Z).\] Then Theorem~\ref{theorem:equivariant cohomology contact} follows from Theorem 4.8 in \cite{DJ}.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the two homotopy equivalences down to $H^{*}_{T^m}(P^{\mu})$ and quote Davis-Januszkiewicz.

nodes.name: $H^{1}(M;\Z)=0$ for a good contact toric manifold
nodes.statement: For a good contact toric manifold $M$, we have $H^{1}(M;\Z)=0$.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
assumptions: For a good contact toric manifold $M$

nodes.name: Proof that $H^{1}(M;\Z)=0$
nodes.statement: Consider the spectral sequence of the fiber bundle \begin{equation} M\hookrightarrow ET^n\times_{T^n}M \rightarrow BT^n \end{equation} If $E_{2}^{0,1}=H^{1}(M;\Z)$ has torsion, it will be in the kernel of \begin{equation} d_{2}: E_{2}^{0,1}\rightarrow E_{2}^{2,0} \end{equation} since $E_{2}^{2,0}=H^{2}(BT^n;\Z)=\Z^n$ is free. So the torsion part will live to $E_{\infty}^{0,1}$. Thus $H^{1}(ET^n\times_{T^n}M;\Z)$ will have torsion and contradicts Theorem~\ref{theorem:equivariant cohomology contact}, from which it easily follows that $H^{1}(ET^n\times_{T^n}M;\Z)=0$. So $H^{1}(M;\Z)$ is torsion-free. Theorem 1.1 in \cite{L:homotopy group} tells us that $\pi_{1}(M)$ is a finite group. So $H_{1}(M;\Z)$ is finite, and $H^{1}(M;\Z)$ has no free part. Thus, we may conclude that $H^{1}(M;\Z)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Serre spectral sequence rules out torsion, and finiteness of $\pi_1(M)$ rules out a free part.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds

nodes.name: Finiteness of $\pi_{1}(M)$ for $K$-contact toric manifolds
nodes.statement: Theorem 1.1 in \cite{L:homotopy group} tells us that $\pi_{1}(M)$ is a finite group.
nodes.section: 3 Equivariant cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
nodes.origin_citation: Lerman, Homotopy groups of $K$-contact toric manifolds

nodes.name: the maps $\pi_{\Z},\pi_{\R},\pi_{T}$ and $K$ for a Delzant polytope
nodes.statement: Then define a map \begin{equation} \pi_{\Z}: \Z^m\rightarrow \Z^k \end{equation} by sending the $i^{th}$ standard basis vector $e_{i}$ of $\Z^m$ to $\tilde{v_{i}}$. This induces a map \begin{equation} \pi_{\R}: \R^m\rightarrow \R^k \end{equation} by tensoring with $\R$. We then get a map \begin{equation} \pi_{T}: T^m=\R^m/\Z^m \rightarrow T^k=\R^k/\Z^k \end{equation} The subscripts $\Z,\R,T$ will be omitted sometimes when it will not cause confusion. Letting $K=ker(\pi_{T})$, we have a short exact sequence of groups \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ 1 \ar[r]^{} & K \ar[r]^{i} & T^m \ar[r]^{\pi_{T}} & T^k \ar[r]^{} & 1. }

nodes.statement: Then \begin{equation} N=((i^*\circ u)^{-1}(i^{*}(-\eta)))/K \end{equation} is the symplectic toric manifold associated to the polytope $P$, where $\eta=(\eta_{1},...,\eta_{m})\in \R^m= (\mathfrak{t}^m)^*$.
nodes.statement_short: $N$ is the symplectic reduction $((i^*\circ u)^{-1}(i^*(-\eta)))/K$ of $\C^m$.

nodes.statement: This action is Hamiltonian with moment map \begin{eqnarray} \nu: & N& \rightarrow (\mathfrak{t}^k)^{*}\\ &[z_{1},...,z_{m}]& \mapsto (\pi^{*})^{-1}(u(z_{1},...,z_{m})+\eta), \end{eqnarray} using that $\pi^{*}$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: $\nu[z]=(\pi^{*})^{-1}(u(z)+\eta)$ is the moment map of $T^k$ on $N$, with image $P$.

conclusions: $P^{\tilde{\lambda}}$ is $T^{k}$-equivariantly homeomorphic to $N$, the symplectic manifold associated to $P$

nodes.statement: The following diagram was used in \cite{DJ} to compute $H^{*}(N;\Z)=H^{*}((T^k\times P)/\tilde{\Delta};\Z)$. \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ N\ar[r]^(0.4){f_1} & ET^k\times_{T^k}N & ET^m\times_{T^m}((T^m\times P)/\Omega) \ar[l]_(0.6){f_2} \ar[r]^(0.6){f_3} & ET^m\times_{T^m}pt}.

nodes.statement: Taking cohomology of diagram~\eqref{eq:diagram sym orb} allows us to compute the equivariant cohomology of the symplectic toric manifold \begin{equation} H_{T^k}^{*}(N;\Z)=H^{*}(ET^k\times_{T^k}(T^k\times P)/\tilde{\Delta});\Z)= \Z[x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{m}]/\I\ , \end{equation} where $x_{i}\in H_{T^k}^{2}(N;\Z)$, $1\leq i\leq m$, are images of generators of $H^{*}(ET^m\times_{T^m}pt, \Z)$. And the ideal $\I$ was defined in Definition~\ref{def:I}.

nodes.name: the linear forms $J_{i}$ and the ideal $\J$
nodes.statement: Suppose $\tilde{v_{j}}=(v_{j1},v_{j2},...,v_{jk})$, for $1\leq j\leq m$. Let \begin{equation}J_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}v_{ji}x_{j}, \end{equation} for $1\leq i\leq k$. We define \begin{equation} \J=\langle J_{1},J_{2},...,J_{k}\rangle \end{equation} to be the ideal in $\Q[x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{m}]$ generated by the linear terms $\{J_{1},J_{2},...,J_{k}\}$.

nodes.name: $T^r$-equivariant cohomology of $N$
nodes.statement_short: Restricting to a subtorus $T^r$ only kills the first $k-r$ linear forms $J_i$.

assumptions: If we denote by $T^r$ the subgroup of $T^k=(S^1)^k$ that is the last $r$ copies of $S^1$, then the $T^k$ action on $N$ restricts to a $T^r$ action on $N$

nodes.name: Proof of the $T^r$-equivariant cohomology corollary
nodes.statement: The spectral sequence of the singular cohomology with $\Z$ coefficients of the fiber bundle \begin{equation*} N\hookrightarrow ET^r\times_{T^r}N\rightarrow BT^r \end{equation*} degenerates at the $E^{2}$ term, since both $N$ and $BT^r$ have cohomology only in even degrees. Thus $ET^r\times_{T^r} N$ also has cohomology only in even degrees. Denote by $T^{k-r}$ the subgroup of $T^k$ that is the product of the first $k-r$ copies of $S^1$ in $T^k= (S^1)^k$. We complete the proof by applying the argument in Theorem 4.14 in \cite{DJ} to the fiber bundle \begin{equation*} ET^r\times_{T^r}N \hookrightarrow ET^{k-r}\times_{T^{k-r}}(ET^r\times_{T^r}N)\rightarrow BT^{k-r} \end{equation*} and also noticing that $ET^{k-r}\times_{T^{k-r}}(ET^r\times_{T^r}N)=ET^k\times_{T^k}N$.
nodes.statement_short: Even-degree cohomology forces the spectral sequence to degenerate; then apply the Davis-Januszkiewicz argument to the residual $T^{k-r}$-bundle.

nodes.name: Cones differing by $SL(n;\Z)$ give contactomorphic manifolds
nodes.statement: The good contact toric manifolds associated to two cones that differ by a transformation in $SL(n;\Z)$ are contactomorphic. This fact was not stated in \cite{L:contact toric}, but it easily follows from the classification theorem there.

nodes.name: Equivalent characterizations of $C_{0}\subset U\R^n$
nodes.statement: The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $C_{0}\subset U\R^n$,where $U\R^n$ stands for the `upper half space': $\{(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})\in \R^n:x_{n}>0\}.$ \item $(0,0,...,0,1)\in (C^{\vee})^{\circ}$, where $C^{\vee}=\{y\in \R^n: \langle y, x\rangle \geq 0, \forall x\in C\}$, and $(C^{\vee})^{\circ}$ is its interior $\{y\in \R^n: \langle y, x\rangle > 0, \forall x\in C_{0}\}$. \item $(0,0,...,0,1)$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{v_{i},1\leq i\leq m\}$ with positive coefficients. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $C_0$ lies in the upper half space iff $(0,\dots,0,1)$ is interior to the dual cone iff it is a positive combination of the $v_i$.

conclusions: $C_{0}\subset U\R^n$,where $U\R^n$ stands for the `upper half space': $\{(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})\in \R^n:x_{n}>0\}.$

nodes.name: Proof of the equivalent characterizations
nodes.statement: Denote $(0,0,...,0,1)$ by $\vec{a}$. (\ref{item: def of A})$\Rightarrow$(\ref{item: dual cone}): For any $x\in C_{0}, \langle \vec{a}, x\rangle =x_{n} > 0$. (\ref{item: dual cone})$\Rightarrow$(\ref{item:linear combi}): The dual cone $C^{\vee}$ is spanned by rays along $v_{1},v_{2},...,v_{m}$. So any vector in the interior of it can be expressed as linear combination of $\{v_{i},1\leq i\leq m\}$ with positive coefficients. (\ref{item:linear combi})$\Rightarrow$(\ref{item: def of A}): For any $x\in C$, we have $\langle x, v_{i}\rangle \geq 0$, for $1\leq i\leq m$, with all equalities if and only if $x=\vec{0}$. Suppose \begin{equation*} \vec{a}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}k_{i}v_{i}, \mbox{with}\ k_{i}>0\ \forall i.\end{equation*} Then \begin{equation*}x_{n}=\langle x, \vec{a}\rangle= \sum_{i=1}^{m}k_{i}\langle x, v_{i}\rangle \geq 0.\end{equation*} The equality holds if and only if $x=\vec{0}$. So for any $x\in C_{0}, x_{n}>0$, i.e., $C_{0}\subset U\R^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Cyclic chain of three implications using the dual cone and positivity of $\langle x,v_i\rangle$.

nodes.name: A good cone can be moved into the upper half space
nodes.statement: There is an element $B$ in $SL(n;\Z)$ so that $B(C_{0})$ is in $U\R^n$.
nodes.section: 5 The singular cohomology of good contact toric manifolds
assumptions: Given a strictly convex good cone
conclusions: There is an element $B$ in $SL(n;\Z)$ so that $B(C_{0})$ is in $U\R^n$.

nodes.name: Proof that a good cone can be moved into the upper half space
nodes.statement: Let $v=\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{i}$ and $u$ be the primitive vector in the direction of $v$. Suppose \begin{equation*} u=\frac{1}{k}v, \mbox{for}\ k\in \Z_{>0}. \end{equation*} Since $u$ is primitive, there exists $D\in SL(n,\Z)$, such that, $D(u)=(0,0,...,0,1)$. Define a transformation $B$ of $\R^n$ by: \begin{equation} x\mapsto Bx= D^{T}x , \end{equation} where the matrix for $D^{T}$ is the transpose of the matrix for $D$. Since $det D^{T}=det D=1$, we still have $B\in SL(n;\Z)$. Under this transformation $B$, the cone $C = \bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in \R^n: \langle x, v_{i}\rangle \geq 0\}$ is taken to \begin{equation}B(C)= \bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in \R^n: \langle x, D(v_{i})\rangle \geq 0\}.\end{equation} So the normal vectors to the facets of the new cone $B(C)$ are $\{D(v_{i}):1\leq i\leq m\}$. Moreover, \begin{equation} (0,0,...,0,1)=D(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{1}{k}D(v_{i}). \end{equation} Finally, using Lemma~\ref{lemma:equiva of Assu A}, we see that the new cone $B(C_{0})$ is in $U\R^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Send the primitive vector along $\sum_i v_i$ to $(0,\dots,0,1)$ by some $D\in SL(n,\Z)$ and take $B=D^T$.

nodes.name: the facets $\tilde{F_{i}}$ of $P$ and their normals $\tilde{v_{i}}$
nodes.statement: The intersection of facet $F_{i}$ with $H$ is given by \[\tilde{F_{i}}:=\left\{(x_{1},...,x_{n-1},1)\in \R^n:\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}x_{j}v_{ij}+v_{in} \geq 0\right\}.\] Let $\F= \{\tilde{F_{i}}:1\leq i\leq m\}$. If we identify $H$ with $\R^{n-1}$ via \[(x_{1},...,x_{n-1},1)\mapsto (x_{1},...,x_{n-1}),\] then $P$ can be thought of as a polytope in $\R^{n-1}$ given by \begin{equation} \{x\in \R^{n-1}: \langle x,\tilde{v_{i}}\rangle \geq -v_{in}\}, \end{equation} where $\tilde{v_{i}}=(v_{i1},...,v_{i,n-1})$ is normal to $\tilde{F_{i}}$ in $H=\R^{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Slicing the cone at $x_n=1$ realizes $P\subset\R^{n-1}$ with facet normals $\tilde{v_{i}}=(v_{i1},\dots,v_{i,n-1})$ and offsets $-v_{in}$.

nodes.name: Smoothness Criterion
nodes.statement: {\bf Smoothness Criterion}: The polytope $P$ is a Delzant polytope in $\R^{n-1}$ and $\tilde{v_{i}}$ is a primitive vector in $\Z^{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $P$ is Delzant in $\R^{n-1}$ and every $\tilde{v_{i}}$ is primitive in $\Z^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Scope of the smoothness criterion
nodes.statement: This assumption allows us to stay in the smooth category in the following discussion. In general, $P$ is just a simple rational convex polytope, not necessarily smooth, so the results in this section do not hold in full generality. However, if we only care about rational cohomology, the argument and theorems in this section will still be valid in general. In that case, we need to use toric orbifolds instead of manifolds, and $S^1$ orbi-bundles instead of ``honest'' $S^1$ bundles.
nodes.statement_short: Without smoothness the section's results still hold rationally, but with orbifolds and orbi-bundles.

nodes.name: $M$ is a principal $S^{1}$-bundle over $N$
nodes.statement: With the notation as above, the good contact toric manifold $M$ is a principal $S^{1}$ bundle over $N$. The projection map \[d: M=(T^n\times P)/\Delta \rightarrow N=(T^{n-1}\times P)/\widetilde{\Delta}\] is given by \[[t,p]\mapsto [\tilde{t},p],\] where $t=(e^{i\theta_{1}},e^{i\theta_{2}},...,e^{i\theta_{n}})\in T^n$, and $\tilde{t}=(e^{i\theta_{1}},e^{i\theta_{2}},...,e^{i\theta_{n-1}})\in T^{n-1}$ is just $t$ with the last coordinate dropped. The notation $[t,p]$ and $[\tilde{t},p]$ refers to the equivalence classes of $(t,p)$ and $(\tilde{t},p)$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Dropping the last torus coordinate exhibits $M$ as a principal $S^1$-bundle over the symplectic toric manifold $N$.

conclusions: the good contact toric manifold $M$ is a principal $S^{1}$ bundle over $N$

nodes.name: Proof that $M\to N$ is a principal $S^{1}$-bundle
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} S^1=\{(1,1,...,1,e^{i\theta_{n}})\in T^n: \theta_{n}\in \R\} \end{equation} act on $M=(T^n\times P)/\Delta$ by multiplication on $T^n$. Because of the smoothness criterion we imposed, $S^1\cap \Delta_{p}=1$, for any $p\in P$, and so this action is free. The quotient space is \begin{equation} (T^n\times P)/\langle \Delta, S^1\rangle = (T^n\times P)/\langle \widetilde{\Delta}, S^1 \rangle = (T^n/S^1\times P)/\widetilde{\Delta} = (T^{n-1}\times P)/\widetilde{\Delta}. \end{equation} Therefore $N$ is the orbit space, and from the construction, we can see the map from the space $M$ to $N$ just drops the last coordinate of $t$.
nodes.statement_short: The last $S^1$ factor acts freely by the smoothness criterion, and its quotient is exactly $N$.

nodes.name: Gysin sequence of the $S^{1}$-bundle $d:M\to N$
nodes.statement: From this perspective, then, we get the Gysin sequence of the $S^1$-bundle, namely the long exact sequence: \[ \xymatrix{ \ar[r]^{} & H^{2k-1}(N;\Z) \ar[r]^{\cup e} & H^{2k+1}(N;\Z) \ar[r]^{d^{*}} & H^{2k+1}(M;\Z) \ar[r]^{d_{*}} & H^{2k}(N;\Z)\ar`r[d]`[l] `[lllld]_{\cup e}`[dlll][dlll] &\\ &H^{2k+2}(N;\Z) \ar[r]^{d^{*}} & H^{2k+2}(M;\Z) \ar[r]^{d_{*}} & H^{2k+1}(N;\Z) \ar[r]^{\cup e}& H^{2k+3}(N;\Z) \ar[r] & }
nodes.statement_short: The long exact sequence alternating $\cup e$, $d^{*}$ and the Gysin map $d_{*}$.

nodes.name: Push-pull (projection) formula for the Gysin map
nodes.statement: The map $d_{*}$ is the map commonly called {\em Gysin map}. It is not a ring homomorphism, but it is a $H^{*}(N;\Z)$-module homomorphism in the following sense: \begin{equation} d_{*}(d^{*}\alpha \cup \beta)= \alpha\cup d_{*}(\beta), \end{equation} for $\alpha\in H^{*}(N;\Z)$ and $\beta\in H^{*}(M;\Z)$.
nodes.statement_short: $d_{*}(d^{*}\alpha\cup\beta)=\alpha\cup d_{*}(\beta)$, so $d_{*}$ is $H^{*}(N;\Z)$-linear.

nodes.name: Grouped short exact sequence for $H^{even}$ and $H^{odd}$
nodes.statement: Put together the exact sequences \eqref{eq:ses} of different degrees, we get the following exact sequence: \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r]^{} & H^{odd}(M;\Z) \ar[r]^{d_{*}} & H^{*}(N;\Z) \ar[r]^{\cup e} & H^{*}(N;\Z) \ar[r]^{d^{*}} & H^{even}(M;\Z) \ar[r]^{} & 0 }.
nodes.statement_short: $0\to H^{odd}(M)\to H^{*}(N)\xrightarrow{\cup e}H^{*}(N)\to H^{even}(M)\to 0$.

nodes.name: even and odd parts of $H^{*}(M;\Z)$
nodes.statement: Define the even part of $H^{*}(M;\Z)$ as \begin{equation}H^{even}(M;\Z)=: \{\alpha\in H^{k}(M;\Z): k \ is\ an\ even\ integer\}.\end{equation} Define the odd part of $H^{*}(M;\Z)$ as \begin{equation}H^{odd}(M;\Z)=: \{\alpha\in H^{k}(M;\Z): k\ is\ an\ odd\ integer\}.\end{equation}

nodes.name: $H^{even}$ is a subring and $H^{odd}$ a module over it
nodes.statement: It's easy to see that $H^{even}(M;\Z)$ is a subring of $H^{*}(M;\Z)$, while $H^{odd}(M;\Z)$ is a module over $H^{even}(M;\Z)$.

nodes.name: $H^{even}(M)\cong\mathrm{coker}\,\rho$ and $H^{odd}(M)\cong\ker\rho$
nodes.statement: Denote by $\rho$ the map \[\cup e: H^{*}(N;\Z)\rightarrow H^{*}(N;\Z).\] Then \begin{equation} H^{even}(M;\Z)\simeq coker\rho = H^{*}(N;\Z)/\langle e\rangle, \end{equation} where $\langle e\rangle$ stands for the ideal of $H^{*}(N;\Z)$ generated by the Euler class $e$. This is a ring isomorphism, and it preserves the degree of the cohomology classes since it is induced by the ring map $d^{*}$. Moreover, \begin{equation} H^{odd}(M;\Z)\simeq ker\rho = Ann(e), \end{equation} where $Ann(e)$ denotes the annihilator of $e$ in $H^{*}(N;\Z)$. This isomorphism maps a cohomology class in $H^{2k+1}(M;\Z)$ to a cohomology class in $H^{2k}(N;\Z)$, lowering the degree by 1. It is an $H^{even}(M;\Z)$-module isomorphism in the following sense. The odd cohomology $H^{odd}(M;\Z)$ is an $H^{even}(M;\Z)$-module. Moreover, $ker\rho = Ann(e)$ is an $coker\rho = H^{*}(N;\Z)/\langle e\rangle$-module in the natural way, so it is also an $H^{even}(M;\Z)$-module via the identification of $coker\rho$ and $H^{even}(M;\Z)$ given in \eqref{eq:H_e}. The isomorphism in \eqref{eq:H_o} respects these module structures.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplication by the Euler class has cokernel $H^{even}(M;\Z)$ (as rings) and kernel $H^{odd}(M;\Z)$ (as modules, with a degree shift).

conclusions: H^{even}(M;\Z)\simeq coker\rho = H^{*}(N;\Z)/\langle e\rangle,
H^{odd}(M;\Z)\simeq ker\rho = Ann(e),

nodes.name: Proof of the cokernel/kernel description
nodes.statement: The isomorphism \eqref{eq:H_e} follows from the exactness of \eqref{eq:grouped ses} at the second $H^{*}(N;\Z)$ and $H^{even}(M;\Z)$ and also the fact that $d^{*}: H^{*}(N;\Z)\rightarrow H^{even}(M;\Z)$ is a ring homomorphism. As for \eqref{eq:H_o}, first notice that it follows from \eqref{eq:push-pull} that the map \begin{equation} d_{*}: H^{odd}(M;\Z)\rightarrow H^{*}(N;\Z) \end{equation} is a $H^{*}(N;\Z)$-module homomorphism. Exactness of \eqref{eq:grouped ses} at $H^{odd}(M;\Z)$ and the first $H^{2k}(N;\Z)$ shows that \begin{equation} d_{*}: H^{odd}(M;\Z)\rightarrow ker\rho \end{equation} is an $H^{*}(N;\Z)$-module isomorphism, hence an $H^{*}(N;\Z)/\langle e\rangle$-module isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Read both isomorphisms off the exactness of the grouped sequence, using the projection formula for module structures.

nodes.name: the map $\tilde{\pi}$, the torus $\tilde{K}$ and the splitting $\tilde{r}$
nodes.statement: Define $\tilde{\pi_{\Z}}: \Z^m\rightarrow \Z^{n-1}$ by mapping the $i^{th}$ standard basis vector $e_{i}$ of $\Z^m$ to $\tilde{v_{i}}$. This induces a map \begin{equation} \tilde{\pi}: T^m\rightarrow T^{n-1}. \end{equation} in the same way we defined $\pi_{T}$ in \eqref{eq:pi_T}. Let $\tilde{K}=ker \tilde{\pi}$. Since $P$ is Delzant and $\tilde{v_{i}}$ is primitive, $\tilde{K}$ is connected, and there exists a splitting $\tilde{r}: T^m\rightarrow \tilde{K}$ such that $\tilde{r}|_{\tilde{K}}=id_{\tilde{K}}$.

nodes.name: the spaces $L_{1},L_{2},L_{3}$ and the weight vector $\vec{v^l}$
nodes.statement: We will use the following diagram to compute the Euler class $e$. { \[\xymatrix{ M \ar[d]_{d} & L_{1}=ET^{n-1}\times_{T^{n-1}}M \ar[d]_{d_{1}} & L_{2} \ar[d]_{d_{2}} & L_{3}=ET^m\times_{T^m}S^1 \ar[d]^{d_{3}} \\ N \ar[r]^(.3){f_{1}} & ET^{n-1}\times_{T^{n-1}}N & (E\tilde{K}\times ET^{n-1})\times_{T^m}P^{\mu} \ar[l]_{f_{2}} \ar[r]^(0.6){f_{3}} & ET^{m}\times_{T^m}pt }\] } The base spaces and the maps are virtually the same as that of \eqref{eq:diagram sym orb}. An element $t_m\in T^m$ acts on $E\tilde{K}\times ET^{n-1}$ via the diagonal action of $(\tilde{r}(t_m), \tilde{\pi}(t_m))$. We now turn to the top line. On $L_{1}$, $T^{n-1}\circlearrowright M= (T^{n}\times P)/\Delta$ by multiplication of $T^{n-1}$ on the first $n-1$ coordinates of $T^{n}$. On $L_{3}$, $T^{m}\circlearrowright S^{1}$ with weight $-(v_{1n},v_{2n},...,v_{mn})$. We will use $\vec{v^l}$ to denote the vector $(v_{1n},v_{2n},...,v_{mn})$. Finally, $L_{2}$ is defined as the pull-back $f_{2}^{*}(L_{1})$.
nodes.statement_short: A diagram of $S^1$-bundles over the Davis-Januszkiewicz zig-zag, with $L_3=ET^m\times_{T^m}S^1$ of weight $-\vec{v^l}$.

nodes.name: Identification of the pull-backs of $L_{1}$ and $L_{3}$
nodes.statement: As principal-$S^{1}$-bundles over $N$, \begin{equation} f_{1}^{*}(L_{1})=M. \end{equation} As principal $S^{1}$-bundles over $(E\tilde{K}\times ET^{n-1})\times_{T^m}P^{\mu}$, \begin{equation} L_{2}=f_{2}^{*}L_{1}= f_{3}^{*}L_{3}.

nodes.name: Proof of the pull-back identification
nodes.statement: The map $f_{1}$ is an inclusion, so the pull back of $L_{1}$ by $f_{1}$ is just by restriction. Then the equation \eqref{eq:f_1} follows from the definition. To show \eqref{eq:L_2}, it's enough if we can construct an $S^1$-equivariant map from $f_{3}^{*}L_{3}$ to $f_{2}^{*}L_{1}$ , which lifts the identity map of the base space $(E\tilde{K}\times ET^{n-1})\times_{T^m}P^{\mu}$. Let $q= [x,y,[e^{i\vec{\theta}},p]]$ be a point in the base space $(E\tilde{K}\times ET^{n-1})\times_{T^m}P^{\mu}$, where $x\in E\tilde{K}, y\in ET^{n-1}, \vec{\theta}=(\theta_{1},...,\theta_{m}), e^{i\vec{\theta}}=(e^{i\theta_{1}},...,e^{i\theta_{m}})\in T^m$, and $p\in P$. The fiber of $f_{3}^{*}L_{3}$ over the point $q$ is, by the definition of pull-back, the fiber of $L_{3}$ over the point $f_{3}(q)=[(x,y),pt]$, namely \begin{equation} f_{3}^{*}L_{3}|_{q}=\{[(x,y), e^{i\beta}]:\beta\in \R\}. \end{equation} The fiber of $f_{2}^{*}L_{1}$ over the point $q$ is, by the definition of pull-back, the fiber of $L_{1}$ over the point $f_{2}(q)=[y,[ \tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\theta}}),p]]$, namely \begin{equation} f_{2}^{*}L_{1}|_{q}=\{[y,[(\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\theta}}),e^{i\alpha}),p]]: \alpha\in \R\}. \end{equation} Define a map from $f_{3}^{*}L_{3}|_{q}$ to $f_{2}^{*}L_{1}|_{q}$ by sending \begin{equation} [x,y, e^{i\beta}]\mapsto [y,[(\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\theta}}),e^{i\beta+i\langle \vec{v^{l}},\vec{\theta}\rangle}),p]]. \end{equation} We call this map $s_{q}$. To show $s_{q}$ is well-defined, we need to show the definition is independent of the choice of representative of $q$. First, assume $e^{i\vec{\phi}}\in T^m$, and so \begin{equation} [x,y,[e^{i\vec{\theta}},p]]=[\tilde{r}(e^{i\vec{\phi}})x,\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\phi}})y,[e^{i(\vec{\theta}+\vec{\phi})},p]]. \end{equation} Using this representative of $q$, then \begin{eqnarray*} s_{q}([x,y,e^{i\beta}])& = & s_{q}([\tilde{r}(e^{i\vec{\phi}})x,\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\phi}})y, e^{i(\beta+\langle -\vec{v^{l}},\vec{\phi}\rangle)}])\\ & = & [\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\phi}})y,[(\tilde{\pi}(e^{i(\vec{\theta}+\vec{\phi})}),e^{i\beta-i\langle \vec{v^{l}},\vec{\phi}\rangle +i\langle\vec{v^{l}},(\vec{\theta}+\vec{\phi}) \rangle}),p]]\\ & = & [\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\phi}})y,[(\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\phi}})\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\theta}}),e^{i\beta+i\langle \vec{v^{l}},\vec{\theta}\rangle}),p]]. \end{eqnarray*} This equals to the RHS of \eqref{eq:3} by the definition of $L_{1}$ as given before Lemma~\ref{lemma:digram Euler}. Second, choose a different representative by letting $e^{i\vec{\delta}}\in \Omega_{p}$, and then \begin{equation} [x,y,[e^{i\vec{\theta}},p]]=[x,y,[e^{i\vec{\delta}}e^{i\vec{\theta}},p]]. \end{equation} Using this representative of $q$, we have: \begin{eqnarray*} s_{q}([(x,y),e^{i\beta}]) & = & [y,[(\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\delta}}e^{i\vec{\theta}}),e^{i\beta+i\langle \vec{v^{l}},\vec{\delta}+\vec{\theta}\rangle}),p]]\\ & = & [y,[(\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\delta}})\cdot\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\theta}}),e^{i\langle\vec{v^l},\vec{\delta}\rangle}\cdot e^{i\beta+i\langle\vec{v^l},\vec{\theta}\rangle}),p]]. \end{eqnarray*} This also equals to the RHS of \eqref{eq:3} since \begin{equation} (\tilde{\pi}(e^{i\vec{\delta}}),e^{i\langle\vec{v^l},\vec{\delta}\rangle})\in \Delta_{p}, \end{equation} which is true by definition of $\Delta, \widetilde{\Delta}$ and $\vec{v^l}$. So the map $s_{q}$ defined by \eqref{eq:3} is well-defined. It's obviously $S^{1}$-equivariant.
nodes.statement_short: Build a fibrewise $S^1$-equivariant map $s_q$ between the two pull-backs and check it is independent of the representative of $q$.

nodes.statement: Since the Euler class of $L_{3}$ is $\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{in}x_{i}$, using Lemma~\ref{lemma:digram Euler} and the naturality of Euler classes, we conclude \begin{equation} e=\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{in}x_{i}.

nodes.name: the linear forms $J_{k}$ and the ideals $\J$, $\widetilde{\J}$
nodes.statement: We define linear forms \begin{equation} J_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{ik}x_{i}, 1\leq k\leq n, \end{equation} and the ideals \begin{equation} \J = \langle J_{1},\cdots,J_{n-1},J_{n}\rangle \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \widetilde{\J}=\langle J_{1},\cdots,J_{n-1}\rangle, \end{equation} where $\langle S \rangle$ denotes the ideal in $\Z[x_{1},...,x_{m}]$ generated by the elements of $S$.

nodes.name: Singular cohomology ring of a good contact toric manifold
nodes.statement: Assume \begin{equation} C= \bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in \R^n: \langle x, v_{i}\rangle \geq 0\} \end{equation} is a strictly convex good cone and $M$ is the good contact toric manifold associated with it. Further assume that $C_{0}=C\backslash\{\vec{0}\}\subset U\R^n$ and the smoothness criterion for $C$ holds. Let \begin{equation}\rho:\frac{\Z[x_{1},...,x_{m}]}{\langle \mathcal {I},\widetilde{\J} \rangle}\rightarrow \frac{\Z[x_{1},...,x_{m}]}{\langle \mathcal {I},\widetilde{\J}\rangle} \end{equation} be multiplication by $J_{n}$. Then: \begin{equation} H^{even}(M;\Z)\simeq coker\rho\simeq \Z[x_{1},...,x_{m}]/\langle \I,\J \rangle\end{equation} as rings, where $x_{i}$ represents a cohomology class of degree two. Moreover, \begin{equation} H^{odd}(M;\Z)\simeq ker\rho \end{equation} as $(H^{even}(M;\Z)\simeq coker\rho)$-modules. A homogeneous polynomial of degree $k$ represents a cohomology class of degree $2k+1$ under this isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Under the smoothness criterion, $H^{even}(M;\Z)\cong\Z[x]/\langle\I,\J\rangle$ and $H^{odd}(M;\Z)\cong\ker(\cdot J_n)$, with a degree shift.

nodes.statement: According to Theorem 6.3 in \cite{Guillemin:Kaehler form}, the cohomology class of the K$\ddot{a}$hler form on $N$ is given by \begin{equation} [\omega]=2\pi\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{in}D_{i}, \end{equation} where $D_{i}$ denotes the cohomology class in $H^{2}(N;\R)$ that is the Poincare dual to $(T^{n-1}\times \tilde{F_{i}})/\tilde{\Delta}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the vanishing theorem
nodes.statement: According to Theorem 6.3 in \cite{Guillemin:Kaehler form}, the cohomology class of the K$\ddot{a}$hler form on $N$ is given by \begin{equation} [\omega]=2\pi\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{in}D_{i}, \end{equation} where $D_{i}$ denotes the cohomology class in $H^{2}(N;\R)$ that is the Poincare dual to $(T^{n-1}\times \tilde{F_{i}})/\tilde{\Delta}$. According to Proposition~\ref{prop:Poincare dual} in the Appendix, $D_{i}=-x_{i}$. So \begin{equation} [\omega]=-2\pi e. \end{equation} Using the Hard Lefschetz Theorem on $N$, it follows easily from Theorem~\ref{thm:contact cohomology} that \begin{equation}H^{2k+1}(M;\Q)=0 \end{equation} for $\{k\in \N: 1\leq 2k+1\leq n-1\}$, and \begin{equation} H^{2k}(M;\Q)=0 \end{equation} for $\{k\in \N:n\leq 2k\leq 2n-2\}$. Furthermore, as the cohomology ring of a symplectic toric manifold, the ring $\Z[x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{m}]/\{\I,\tilde{\J}\}$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:contact cohomology} is torsion-free (see \cite{toric variety}). Therefore as an ideal of it, $ker\rho$ is also torsion-free. Hence \begin{equation}H^{2k+1}(M;\Z)=0 \end{equation} for $\{k\in \N: 1\leq 2k+1\leq n-1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $[\omega]=-2\pi e$ and apply Hard Lefschetz on $N$, then upgrade $\Q$ to $\Z$ by torsion-freeness.

nodes.name: line-bundle description of $c_{i}$
nodes.statement: The torus $T^m$ acts on $\C^m$ in the standard way and $\C^{m}$ splits \begin{equation} \C^m = \C_{1}\oplus \C_{2}\oplus\cdots \oplus \C_{m}. \end{equation} The torus $K$, as a subgroup of $T^m$, also acts on $\C^m$ and preserves this splitting. Then \begin{equation} (Z\times \C_{i})/K\rightarrow Z/K \end{equation} is a complex line bundle over $N=Z/K$, where the action of $K$ on $\C_{i}$ is by first including $K$ into $T^m$, then acting with weight $-(0,...,0,1,0,...,0)$, where the only $1$ is on the $i^{th}$ position. The $K$ action on $Z\times \C_{i}$ is the diagonal action. Then the first Chern class of this line bundle is $c_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: $c_i$ is the first Chern class of $(Z\times\C_i)/K\to Z/K$, where $K$ acts with weight $-e_i$.
